title: Lambda: Tiny One-Line Functions (and When Not to Use Them)
excerpt: Write short throwaway functions with lambda, use them with sorted(), map() and filter(), and know when a normal def is clearer.

headings.text: A Function You Only Need Once

html:
Some functions are so small and so temporary that giving them a name and a full def block feels like overkill. A typical case is telling sorted() how to rank items: you need a tiny rule, once, and then never again.

A lambda is a small anonymous function (a function without a name) written in a single expression (a piece of code that produces a value, like n * n), ideal for short rules you pass to another function. This lesson shows how it is built, where it is used most, and the limits that tell you when to switch back to def.

A Function You Only Need Once

Sorting words by length requires a rule that turns each word into its length. With a regular function it looks like this:

words = ["banana", "fig", "apple", "kiwi"]

def by_length(word):
    return len(word)

print(sorted(words, key=by_length))
['fig', 'kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']

The key parameter takes a function, and sorted() calls it on every item to decide the order. Notice that you write key=by_length with no parentheses: you pass the function itself rather than calling it. Do you really need a named function for a one-line rule used in one place? That is exactly what lambda is for.

The lambda Syntax

A lambda is written as the word lambda, then the parameters, a colon, and one expression. There is no return; the value of the expression is returned automatically:

print(sorted(words, key=lambda word: len(word)))
['fig', 'kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']

The result is identical to the def version. You can also store a lambda in a variable and call it like any function, and it can take several parameters. (This is fine for a quick demonstration, but once a function has a name, a regular def is usually clearer.)

square = lambda n: n * n
add = lambda a, b: a + b

print(square(7))
print(add(3, 4))
49
7

Sorting Records by One Field

The most common use is sorting items that have several parts. Here each person is a pair of name and age, and the lambda picks the age (person[1] is the second item of the pair, because counting starts at 0):

people = [("Asha", 31), ("Ravi", 25), ("Meena", 38)]

print(sorted(people, key=lambda person: person[1]))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda person: person[1], reverse=True))
[('Ravi', 25), ('Asha', 31), ('Meena', 38)]
[('Meena', 38), ('Asha', 31), ('Ravi', 25)]

With map() and filter()

Two more built-in functions take a function as an argument. map() applies it to every item, and filter() keeps only the items for which it gives True. Both give you results that you view by wrapping them in list():

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

print(list(map(lambda n: n * 10, numbers)))
print(list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, numbers)))
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
[2, 4, 6]

In the second line, n % 2 == 0 asks whether the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero, which is true for even numbers. Both functions return a kind of recipe that works out its results only when asked, which is why they are wrapped in list() here.

The Limits of lambda

A lambda can contain only one expression, so it cannot hold several statements, loops or assignments. A short either-or choice is still possible with a conditional expression, which reads like a sentence:

label = lambda n: "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"

print(label(6))
print(label(7))
even
odd

When should you use def instead? Whenever the function is more than a quick one-liner: if it needs more than one line, if you want to give it a descriptive name, if you want to document it, or if you use it in several places. Notice that the lambda stored in label above would be better written as a regular def, because once a function has a name you might as well use the clearer form. Lambdas are at their best when they are unnamed and passed straight into another function.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonLambdaFunctions.ipynb.

Summary

  • lambda parameters: expression creates a small function with no name; the expression's value is returned.
  • It is most useful as a throwaway rule passed to sorted(), map(), filter() and similar functions.
  • sorted(items, key=lambda item: item[1]) sorts records by one field.
  • map() transforms every item and filter() keeps the items that pass a test; wrap both in list() to see results.
  • A lambda holds a single expression only; use def for anything longer, named or reused.
